title: Día de los Muertos
hook: in Mexico families welcome the dead with marigolds, photos and favorite foods

segments.voice: Yesterday, Qingming, a broom on a hillside. Your line was sweep the tomb. What did you clean, and whose was it? Today, the end of the week, and the dead come to the family's table. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

A small table against the living room wall, and it's filling up. A framed photo of an abuelo in his good hat. Candles. A plate of his favorite food, still warm. A bottle of the soda he liked. Sweet bread. Paper cut into lace in bright colors. And everywhere, orange: marigolds, heaped in pots and scattered in a path of petals across the floor toward the door. Nobody is setting this table for the living. It's for the people who have died, and the family expects them. This is the ofrenda, the offering, for Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead. Today: a feast with guests you can't see.
screen: `A TABLE FILLS UP.` → `A PATH OF MARIGOLDS.` → `THE OFRENDA.`

segments.voice: First, the visit. In the way families describe it, the dead return for these days to be with the people who love them. So the ofrenda isn't a memorial in the usual sense. It's hospitality. You put out a guest's favorite food because a guest is coming. Second, the marigolds. Their color and scent, families say, help guide the dead home, which is why the petals are laid in a path. The photo on the ofrenda says who is expected. The water, the food, the candles say welcome, you must be tired from the journey. Third, the cemetery. Families also go to the graves, clean and decorate them with flowers and candles, and stay, sometimes through the night, eating, talking, playing music. It can look like a party. For the families who keep it this way, it is one, a loving one. Fourth, where it fits. It comes at the start of November, alongside the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls. You met All Souls earlier in this block, the church praying for the dead by name. In Mexico, as the story is often told, those days meet older Indigenous ways of honoring the dead, and families keep it in their own ways. It isn't Halloween. The painted and sugar skulls are smiling, not scary. Now look back at this week. Visiting graves to be reminded. Going home. Knowing how to die. A skull that wanted to stay dead. Life first. A broom on a hillside. And now, a table set for guests. Different peoples, different beliefs, and the same quiet refusal to let the dead become strangers.
screen: `THE DEAD COME TO VISIT.` · `MARIGOLDS SHOW THE WAY.` · `A NIGHT AT THE GRAVES.` · `THIS WEEK, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `THEY VISIT.`

segments.voice: For these two minutes, make a very small ofrenda. Find a photo of someone who has died, on paper or on your phone, and set it where you can see it. Beside it, put a flower if you have one, or a leaf, or a cup of something they liked. Then just sit with them. If they were coming to visit, what would you want to tell them about your year? Let one thing come. You don't have to say it aloud. The bell holds the time.
Ofrenda, the offering table families in Mexico set for Día de los Muertos, with marigolds, photos and their dead's favorite foods. Today's word.
Your line: they visit. Today, leave the photo and the flower out a little longer, and give the person one minute of your company. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: For Día de los Muertos, families in Mexico and in Mexican communities elsewhere build ofrendas at home with photos, marigolds, candles and the dead's favorite foods, and families visit and decorate graves; customs vary by region and family.
